original_question: In the homogeneous Peres-Schlag setting, where a sequence (t_j) satisfies t_{j+1}/t_j >= 1 + 1/M and one seeks a real alpha with all ||alpha t_j|| bounded away from zero, what is the correct order of approximation? More specifically, can Theorem 9 be improved beyond the lower bound gamma/(M log M), and what is the optimal dependence on M in the homogeneous case?
target_in_paper: §1, subsection "Peres-Schlag’s method": the unnumbered open question immediately after Theorem 9 and equation (13), asking for the right order of approximation in the homogeneous version of Theorem 9.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact Peres-Schlag framework used in the paper: a real sequence {t_j} with t_{j+1}/t_j >= 1 + 1/M, the existence problem for a real alpha with all ||alpha t_j|| bounded away from 0, the current lower bound gamma/(M log M) from Theorem 9, and the fact that the paper is asking for the optimal dependence on M specifically in the homogeneous case.
missing_details: The paper does not state this as a numbered conjecture; it is an unnumbered open question immediately after Theorem 9 and equation (13).
You should define ||x|| as the distance from x to the nearest integer.
The ambient objects should be stated explicitly: {t_j} is a sequence of real numbers, indexed by j in Z_+, and alpha is a real number.
The exact quantifiers should be made explicit: for every sequence {t_j} satisfying t_{j+1}/t_j >= 1 + 1/M for all j, does there exist alpha in R such that the stated lower bound holds for all j?
The theorem assumes M > 2; if one asks for the optimal order in M, this should be understood asymptotically as M -> infinity.
To make the question paper-faithful, one should note that 'homogeneous' means the special case with no shifts eta_j, in contrast to the inhomogeneous variant (12).

The paper frames the problem using the explicit obstruction (13): for every large integer M there exists an infinite sequence {t_j} such that for every alpha in R there are infinitely many j with ||alpha t_j|| <= 1/M; this shows the optimal order cannot be better than constant/M up to absolute constants.
The paper also notes that the numerator constant 1 in (13) can be improved, so the real issue is the order in M, not that specific constant.
refined_question: For M > 2, determine the correct order, as M -> infinity, of the best universal lower bound c(M) with the following property: for every sequence of real numbers {t_j}_{j>=1} satisfying t_{j+1}/t_j >= 1 + 1/M for all j >= 1, there exists a real number alpha such that ||alpha t_j|| > c(M) for all j >= 1, where ||x|| denotes distance to the nearest integer. Peres-Schlag’s Theorem 9 gives c(M) >= gamma/(M log M) for some absolute constant gamma > 0, while the example in (13) shows that for every large integer M there are such sequences for which every alpha has ||alpha t_j|| <= C/M for infinitely many j, so the optimal homogeneous order cannot exceed constant/M. Can Theorem 9 be improved, and what is the optimal dependence on M in this homogeneous case (equivalently, is the true order constant/M up to absolute factors, or does an additional logarithmic loss remain unavoidable)?
justification: The draft is targeting the author’s exact open problem in the subsection on Peres-Schlag’s method. The paper first states Theorem 9 with the lower bound gamma/(M log M) under the lacunarity condition t_{j+1}/t_j >= 1 + 1/M, then records the inhomogeneous analogue (12), and then gives an explicit construction leading to (13), which shows that in the homogeneous case one cannot hope for a universal lower bound better than order 1/M up to constants. Immediately after that, the author writes that the open question is to find the right order of approximation in the homogeneous version of the problem and conjectures that Theorem 9 is not optimal. So your draft is very close, but the fully stand-alone version must include the exact quantifiers, define ||·||, specify that the sequence is real-valued, distinguish the homogeneous case from the inhomogeneous one, and include the order-1/M obstruction that is part of the paper’s own framing of the question.
